meta.ogDescription: Not Henry Ford. Quotation researchers trace it to an anonymous 1908–1910 advertising proverb, popularized by 'Abe Martin' in 1916.

answer.label: Not Henry Ford — an anonymous advertising-trade proverb
answer.authorDates: First documented 1908–1910 · anonymous advertising & trade-press saying
answer.sourceLine: There is no evidence Henry Ford said or wrote this. Quotation etymologist Barry Popik traces it to an anonymous advertising- and trade-press proverb: a cigar-ad form appeared in 1908, the ad-specific “stopping an ad to save money is like stopping a clock to save time” in 1910, and Kin Hubbard’s cartoon philosopher “Abe Martin” popularized it in 1916. The Ford (and Thomas Jefferson) credits are later, unsupported add-ons; the smooth “watch” wording is a modern polish with no primary source.

source.excerpt: Stopping an ad to save money is like stopping a clock to save time.
trail: Quotation etymologist Barry Popik documents a 1908 cigar advertisement (“Buying cheap cigars to save money is like stopping the clock to save time”) and, by 1910, the advertising-specific form in the trade paper N.A.R.D. Notes.
Kin Hubbard’s newspaper character “Abe Martin” used it in 1916: “You might as well stop the clock to save time as to stop advertising to save money.”
Popik notes the line is credited to both Ford and Jefferson with no evidence either man said it.
Quote aggregators such as AZQuotes nonetheless print the polished “watch” wording under Henry Ford’s name with no source.
source.excerptNote: The advertising-specific form as cited in the trade publication N.A.R.D. Notes, 28 April 1910 — years before the saying was ever linked to Henry Ford. The now-common “stopping your watch to save time” wording is a later, smoother variant.

source.rightsNote: This is an anonymous advertising-trade saying whose earliest documented forms date to 1908–1910; no single author or first-publication of the exact modern “stopping your watch to save time” wording can be established, so no copyright status is asserted. The underlying proverb circulated freely in the early-20th-century trade press.

author.name: Henry Ford
author.heading: About Henry Ford
author.metaLine: 1863–1947 · American industrialist · founder of the Ford Motor Company
author.bio: Henry Ford pioneered the moving assembly line and the mass-market automobile, making the Model T a household object. Because he is shorthand for hard-headed business sense, motivational and marketing quotes are routinely pinned on him. This advertising aphorism is one of them: it circulated anonymously in the trade press years before his name was attached, and no documented Ford source for it exists.

misattribution.heading: Why Henry Ford gets the credit
misattribution.intro: The line is one of the internet’s favourite “marketing wisdom” quotes, and Ford is the default magnet for pithy business sayings. But the saying is older than its Ford attribution and has no documented Ford source.

items.why: Widely printed under Ford’s name by quote aggregators like AZQuotes, but Barry Popik finds no evidence Ford ever said it, and the proverb predates any Ford link.
Some sites credit Jefferson (d. 1826) instead — an anachronism, since advertising in this sense and the saying itself both postdate him. Popik lists this credit as equally unsupported.

misattribution.truthLine: The earliest datable forms are anonymous trade-press sayings of 1908–1910, with Kin Hubbard’s “Abe Martin” popularizing the advertising version in 1916 — none of them Henry Ford.

context.heading: An ad-trade proverb, not a Ford maxim
lead: The saying began life as a piece of self-interested advertising-trade rhetoric — a snappy way for publishers and ad sellers to warn businesses against cutting their ad budgets. Its earliest cousins compare cutting corners to stopping a clock to save time, a stock joke that predates the advertising application.

Over the century the wording drifted from “clock” to “watch” and picked up a famous name. Ford’s reputation for blunt commercial common sense made him the natural host, even though the line was in circulation before he was associated with it.
context.pull: Stop the clock to save time, stop advertising to save money — same false economy, and neither line is Ford’s.
